title: If lawmakers deserve privacy, so do their supporters
summary: In the current climate, when anybody can be a target, Maryland lawmakers were right to consider a bill to shield their home addresses from public view, writes David Keating, but they should extend the same protections to small-dollar donors to their campaigns.
content:
by David Keating, Maryland Matters July 16, 2026

by David Keating, Maryland Matters July 16, 2026

The assassination of Minnesota Rep. Melissa Hortman and the attempted murder of state Sen. John Hoffman last June shocked the nation. It reminded us that political violence is a grim reality in today’s polarized climate.

In Annapolis, lawmakers responded with Senate Bill 632 — a measure that would help shield current and former state elected officials and their families from similar dangers. It rightly recognized a core problem of contemporary politics: Easily accessible home addresses can enable harassment and violence. Had it passed, their addresses would no longer be public. No one should have to choose between public service and their family’s safety.

Unfortunately, SB 632 failed to pass. However, it’s likely that lawmakers will revisit this issue at their next opportunity. When they do, as they act to protect their own privacy, they should also protect their supporters.

Current state law leaves tens of thousands of ordinary Marylanders exposed via the mandatory public disclosure of political contributors’ home addresses.

Accessing that information has never been easier. Federal Election Commission Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum, a Democrat, explained that obtaining contributor information in the 1970s meant physically visiting the FEC’s office and paging through paper files. That has changed, she warned, noting that “armed with only an individual’s name, it takes less than a half-dozen clicks on the commission’s website” to locate that person’s home address.

That’s true in Maryland, too.

Rapid technological change has left campaign finance laws dangerously outdated, creating fresh dangers for Americans who support candidates at a time when, sadly, political passions increasingly turn hostile—or violent.

The threat isn’t hypothetical. Investigators found that the Minnesota gunman used data brokers to compile a target list of nearly 70 individuals, getting home addresses with ease. An attacker could easily use public websites to target citizens who supported the “wrong” politician, party or idea.

Under Maryland law, candidate campaign committees must report the name and home address of every contributor —  there is no minimum donation that shields a donor’s personal information from disclosure. This is absurd and potentially dangerous.

There is no legitimate government interest in publishing home addresses — which remain online indefinitely — of someone who gave $100, $20, or even $1 to a candidate. Donations of that size present no risk of corruption, and they tell the public nothing useful about a candidate’s major sources of support. Yet existing law exposes even the smallest contributors to potential harassment, employment discrimination, or worse.

A growing number of states have begun to address this problem. California, Texas, and Wyoming protected donor privacy long ago by withholding street addresses from online disclosure systems. West Virginia and Utah this year enacted laws that protect donors’ personal information.

Minnesota enacted a bill with bipartisan support that redacts donors’ home addresses. Even the pro-campaign-finance-regulation Brennan Center recently came out in support of this common-sense safeguard.

Over 82 million people live in states with such laws, accounting for nearly 25% of the nation’s population.

The bipartisan FEC unanimously recommended that Congress update the disclosure law, to ensure the agency “shall not include the street name and street number of individual contributors in the information it makes available for inspection by the public … and accessible to the public on the Internet.”

The balanced approach endorsed by the FEC and an increasing number of states preserves transparency while protecting safety. Contributors’ names, occupation and employer information, cities, ZIP codes and donation amounts would remain accessible — more than sufficient for meaningful oversight — while removing precise location data that could serve as a road map for targeting.

Maryland should also establish a meaningful disclosure threshold. Currently, there is none, one reason why the state scores poorly in our Free Speech Index, a comprehensive examination of state laws regulating political engagement.

In Maryland, any contribution, however small, triggers public reporting of a donor’s address. For statewide races, disclosure should apply only to substantial contributions—say, $1,000 or more. Raising the threshold would end the unjustified privacy violations affecting small contributors and ease reporting burdens for campaigns that rely on volunteers to track countless minor donations, while maintaining the public’s ability to track genuinely significant financial influences.

Every Marylander deserves the ability to participate in democracy without fear that doing so will put their family at risk. The General Assembly demonstrated exactly this understanding by advancing SB 632 to protect its own members.

When Maryland lawmakers next take up this issue, they should include similar protections for ordinary citizens. If the state whose tragedy sparked a national conversation about lawmaker safety is moving to protect donor addresses, Maryland should take note—and the moment to act is now.
